prompt: A company that recently closed an acquisition needs a KPI scorecard to track the integration program over its first year. Design 4-6 KPIs.
context: Deal rationale (per the approved investment case) was primarily cost synergies from combining back-office functions and secondarily cross-selling the acquired company's product to the acquirer's existing customer base. The investment case assumed $12M/year in run-rate cost synergies by month 18 and an incremental $6M/year in cross-sell revenue by month 24. HR has flagged that voluntary attrition among the acquired company's employees in the first 90 days post-close has historically been a leading indicator of integration trouble at this acquirer, based on 2 prior acquisitions.

binaryCriteria.description: Includes a KPI tracking realized cost-synergy run-rate progress against the specific $12M/year by month-18 target from the investment case.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if cost synergies are not tracked against this specific target.

binaryCriteria.description: Includes a KPI tracking cross-sell revenue progress against the specific $6M/year by month-24 target.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if cross-sell revenue is not tracked against this specific target.

binaryCriteria.description: Includes the acquired company's first-90-days voluntary attrition rate as an explicit early-warning KPI, referencing the acquirer's own historical pattern from prior deals.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if this specific time-bound attrition metric is absent, or only a generic annual attrition/engagement metric is proposed instead.

goldNotes: A strong scorecard tracks progress against the two specific, quantified deal-rationale targets given — cost-synergy run-rate (versus the $12M/month-18 target) and cross-sell revenue (versus the $6M/month-24 target) — as the primary financial KPIs, since these are the actual reasons the deal was approved, not generic "integration health" metrics untethered to the investment case. It should also include the acquired-company voluntary-attrition rate in the first 90 days as an explicit early-warning KPI, directly citing the acquirer's own historical pattern from 2 prior deals as the reason this specific, time-bound metric (not just "annual attrition") is the right one to watch. A weak scorecard proposes only generic M&A-integration metrics (e.g., "employee satisfaction") without connecting to the two specific investment-case targets or the acquirer's own attrition-timing precedent.
